Maladaptive Strategies.value: I detach myself from the memories
become overly compliant when feeling threatened
try hard not think about the trauma

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I remember the event I feel intense rage

Negative Appraisals.value: You can never know who will harm you
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: For a male torture survivor, sexual-trauma-specific verbal cues are possible only if sexual torture or sexual humiliation is part of the trauma, but the rest of the profile provides no corresponding sexual content in memory, appraisals, threat, or coping. As selected, this trigger appears disconnected from the trauma representation and is hard to justify clinically.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: The appraisal that others can visibly see what happened to him implies shame/marked visible contamination or exposure. That could occur after torture, but here it is not supported by the memory items, trigger content, or other appraisals, making it feel mismatched with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: Gambling as a coping strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is poorly linked to the active formulation. The main connected pattern is triggers ↔ negative appraisals with memory-linked re-experiencing and threat-driven compliance/detachment. Gambling introduces a separate excitement-seeking coping style that is not reflected elsewhere and feels clinically disconnected rather than integrated.

vignette: Eduardo had been sixty-two when the men took him. It began in the courtyard of the detention center, where the iron gates sealed behind him with a heavy, final clack. He remembered the way the concrete walls closed in, how the narrow alley offered only two exits, both already guarded. When the first blow struck his shoulder, he had braced for more, but what frightened him most was the absolute lack of a way out. He stood his ground, yet could not step forward or back, trapped by the weight of the men and the narrowing space. A sudden crack echoed from the courtyard gate—a loaded weapon discharging—and the sound did not fade into memory. It arrived in his bones as though it were happening now, loud and immediate, carrying with it the certainty that violence would follow wherever he looked. He had come to believe that the way he had stood, the pause he made before speaking to the officer, was what invited the blows. He told himself he should have moved sooner; his stillness had left him exposed, and he would never forgive himself for that quiet inaction. Over the following years, Eduardo learned to live with a past that refused to stay behind him. When the memories surfaced, he did not fight them; instead, he slipped away from them, watching the images move across his mind like shadows on a wall. He tried hard not to think about the courtyard, the pressure, the crack of the weapon, steering his attention toward the hum of daily routines. Yet when he sat with his grandchildren or spoke at family gatherings, the past would press close. What he dreaded most was not the memories themselves, but the way they arrived unannounced, vivid and unfiltered, making him feel as though he were still standing in that confined space. When he attempted to explain what had happened to the medical workers in his new town, his words would tangle. He would begin with the gate, then the walls, then the sound, but the thread would slip from his hands, and he would leave the story unfinished, his jaw tightening as a quiet rage rose in his chest. He was certain that violence could come from anywhere, and he could never be sure which neighbor, which stranger, which passing car might carry it. His work as a welder grounded his days in the familiar rhythm of metal and flame. The fabrication shop, with its high ceilings and rolling doors, became his daily theater. Yet the environment held its own dangers. When the air compressor hissed and a heavy steel pipe clanged against the concrete floor, Eduardo would freeze, his breath catching as the gunshot noise arrived again, sharp and unyielding. He had grown accustomed to bending to the expectations of his foremen, answering quickly, agreeing to assignments without hesitation, a quiet compliance that settled over him whenever he sensed pressure in the room. This fawning ease occupied the shop floor. His thought suppression followed its own quiet track, running alongside the compliance as he turned his attention toward the torch and the metal. Over the months, he began avoiding the north bay where the steel crates were stacked too close together. He stopped volunteering for the heavy lifts, preferring the open floor where he could step back if the space tightened. The change was subtle but real; his shift pace slowed, and his coworkers learned to give him a wider berth, understanding that the widowed older man needed his breathing room. Now at seventy, with a PCL-5 score of eighty resting on his file, Eduardo sat in the clinician’s office with his hands folded over his knees, the fabric of his shirt still stiff from a morning spent guiding the welding torch. He had come to seek help not because the memories had grown louder, but because the quiet detachment had begun to feel like a slow erosion. He feared that one day he would stop recognizing the world outside the shop, or worse, that the rage he carried for the stillness of those years would finally break through the compliance he wore like a second skin. What he hoped for was simply to stand in a room and know he could step forward or step back, to speak the story of the courtyard without losing the thread, and to let the past finally rest without demanding his forgiveness.
